newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. okays new Iraq oil pricing formulae, contract.
newsitem.headline: U.N. okays new Iraq oil pricing formulae, contract.

text.p: The U.N. sanctions committee on Iraq has approved a new pricing formula for shipping oil into South Africa, and was seen okaying fresh terms for sales into the United States, diplomats said Friday.

"The new U.S. pricing formula was recommended by the overseers and submitted to the sanctions committee today. Under the no-objection procedure it is expected the formula will be approved by Tuesday," said a U.N. official.
The U.N. official would not reveal the new formula.
Pevious terms priced Iraqi barrels into the United States at a five cents discount to Saudi Arab Light.
In a related move, the U.N. recently approved a new contract permitting Hungarian state oil company MOL to take delivery of 1 million barrels of Iraqi crude on a spot basis.
The action marked the 27th contract approved by the U.N.-appointed oil overseers since the oil-for-food plan was enacted on December 10.

Declining world oil prices have forced the overseers to consider spot sales in order to raise the dollar amount of Iraqi crude receipts. Under the oil deal, Baghdad is allowed to sell $1 billion of crude every 90 days over the 180-day period of the plan.

The more than $4 per barrel price slide this past month in oil prices prompted the U.N. to raise the bar on crude contracts. In its latest report, the overseers projected the first tranche of oil receipts to tally out at only around $800 million, some $200 million below the required amount.
The pricing formula for Iraqi barrels into South Africa was set at dated Brent minus $2.15 per barrel for March liftings FOB from the port of Mina al-Bakr, diplomats said.
Committee members met Thursday in an informal, technical level meeting where the pricing formulae were discussed.

In addition, panel members exchanged ideas on how to expedite implemention of the oil-for-food deal. Baghdad has complained in recent days of the slow progress of getting food and supplies into the country.
"There was a philosophical discussion on how do speed this up," said a diplomat.
A formal meeting of the sanctions committee was expected next week, where logistial and theoretical points were to be formalized, the diplomat said.

Under terms of the accord, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of crude over a six-month period in order to alleviate suffering caused by sanctions, clamped on Iraq after it invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
